chapters.1.lds: The 2026 lesson emphasizes God’s presence among exiles. Why does the glory appear among people far from Jerusalem?
chapters.1.summary: Ezekiel is a priest living among the exiles by a river in Babylon. The heavens open, and he sees visions of God. A storm comes from the north with flashing fire. In it are four living creatures, each with four faces and four wings. Beside each is a wheel within a wheel, full of eyes. Above them is a shining platform and a throne like sapphire. On the throne is a figure like a man, surrounded by fire and a rainbow. Ezekiel falls on his face and hears a voice.
chapters.2.lds: The lesson’s opening invites people to hear God’s word. Why must Ezekiel speak even when his listeners refuse?
chapters.2.summary: A voice tells Ezekiel to stand on his feet. The Spirit enters him and sets him upright. God sends him to the people of Israel, a rebellious nation. He must say, “This is what the Lord GOD says.” Whether they listen or not, they will know a prophet was among them. He must not fear them, though they are like thorns and scorpions. He must not be rebellious as they are. A hand holds out a scroll full of mourning and woe.
chapters.3.lds: The lesson connects the watchman’s duty with caring leadership. What makes silence dangerous for the appointed watchman?
chapters.3.summary: Ezekiel eats the scroll, and it is as sweet as honey. God says foreigners would listen, but Israel will not. God makes his forehead as hard as flint. The Spirit carries him to the exiles, and he sits stunned for seven days. Then God makes him a watchman for Israel. If he fails to warn the wicked, he will answer for their blood. If he warns them, he has saved his own life. God then makes him unable to speak except when given a message.
chapters.4.lds: How do measured meals explain the coming siege?
chapters.4.summary: God tells Ezekiel to draw Jerusalem on a clay brick. He must set up a model siege around it. He lies on his left side for 390 days for Israel’s guilt. Then he lies on his right side for forty days for Judah’s. He eats bread made from mixed grains, weighed out each day. He drinks a measured amount of water. He protests at cooking over human waste, and God allows cow dung. God says he will cut off Jerusalem’s supply of bread.
chapters.5.lds: Why do even the protected hairs face a further threat?
chapters.5.summary: God tells Ezekiel to shave his head and beard with a sword. He weighs the hair into three parts. He burns one part inside the model city. He strikes one part with the sword and scatters one to the wind. He tucks a few hairs into his robe and burns some of those. God says this is Jerusalem, set among the nations. She rebelled more than the nations around her. A third die of hunger, a third by sword, and a third are scattered.
chapters.6.lds: How does remembrance change the meaning of survival?
chapters.6.summary: God tells Ezekiel to speak against the mountains of Israel. A sword is coming on the hilltop shrines. Altars will be ruined, and the dead will lie before their idols. Yet God will leave some who escape the sword. Among the nations they will remember him. They will remember how their unfaithful hearts grieved him. They will hate what they did. Then they will know that he is the LORD.
chapters.7.lds: Why can silver no longer provide the security its owners expected?
chapters.7.summary: God says the end has come on the four corners of the land. He will judge the people by their own ways. Violence has grown into a rod of wickedness. Buyers need not rejoice, and sellers need not mourn. The trumpet sounds, and no one goes to battle. The sword is outside, and disease and hunger are inside. People throw their silver into the streets. Prophet, priest, and king have no help to give.
chapters.8.lds: How does the vision answer the elders’ claim that God cannot see?
chapters.8.summary: Ezekiel sits with Judah’s elders in his house in Babylon. A fiery figure lifts him in a vision to Jerusalem’s temple. He sees an idol at the north gate. He digs through a wall and finds seventy elders burning incense to pictures of animals. They say the LORD does not see them. He sees women weeping for the god Tammuz. He sees twenty-five men bowing to the sun with their backs to the temple. God says they have filled the land with violence.
chapters.9.lds: Why does the vision distinguish mourners from other inhabitants?
chapters.9.summary: God calls six men with weapons and one man in linen with a writing kit. The glory of God moves to the temple’s threshold. The man in linen must mark those who grieve over the city’s wrongs. The others are to strike everyone without the mark. They must begin at the sanctuary. Ezekiel falls on his face and asks whether God will destroy all who remain. God answers that the land is full of blood. The man in linen reports that he has done his task.
chapters.10.lds: How does this departure connect with Ezekiel’s opening vision?
chapters.10.summary: Ezekiel sees the sapphire throne above the cherubim again. The man in linen takes burning coals from between the wheels. He is to scatter them over the city. The cloud fills the inner court, and the glory rises to the threshold. Ezekiel describes the wheels and the four-faced creatures once more. He knows them as the creatures he saw by the river in Babylon. The glory leaves the threshold and rests above the cherubim. They rise and stop at the east gate.
chapters.11.lds: Why do distant exiles receive a promise of God’s presence?
chapters.11.summary: At the east gate Ezekiel sees twenty-five leaders who give wicked advice. They say the city is a pot and they are the meat safe inside. God says he will bring them out and judge them. One of them dies while Ezekiel speaks. The people of Jerusalem say the exiles are far from the LORD. God answers that he has been a sanctuary to the exiles. He will gather them and give them one heart and a new spirit. Then the glory leaves the city and stands on the eastern hill.
chapters.12.lds: How does the baggage make a postponed warning immediate?
chapters.12.summary: God tells Ezekiel to pack bags for exile while the people watch. In the evening he digs through the wall and carries his bag out. He covers his face so that he cannot see the land. He tells the people he is a sign for them. Their prince will leave in the dark and be taken to Babylon without seeing it. Ezekiel must eat his bread trembling. People say that visions never come true or concern the distant future. God says none of his words will be delayed any longer.
chapters.13.lds: Why does whitewashed wall imagery fit a false promise of peace?
chapters.13.summary: God speaks against prophets who prophesy from their own minds. They are like foxes among ruins. They have not gone up to repair the gaps in the wall. They say “Peace” when there is no peace. The people build a weak wall, and these prophets cover it with whitewash. Rain, hail, and wind will bring it down. God also speaks against women who sell charms and hunt lives for bread. They discourage the righteous and encourage the wicked.
chapters.14.lds: Why cannot the three righteous figures rescue everyone else?
chapters.14.summary: Some of Israel’s elders come and sit before Ezekiel. God says they have set up idols in their hearts. He asks whether such men should receive an answer. He calls the people to turn from their idols. Then he describes a land that sins and is struck by famine. Even Noah, Daniel, and Job could save only themselves there. They could not save a son or a daughter. Yet some survivors will come out, and their conduct will explain the judgment.
chapters.15.lds: Why does this vine comparison focus on wood instead of fruit?
chapters.15.summary: God asks Ezekiel how vine wood is better than any other wood. No one makes anything from it. No one even takes a peg from it to hang a pot. It is thrown on the fire as fuel. Both ends are burned, and the middle is charred. It was useless whole, and it is more useless burned. God says the people of Jerusalem are like that vine wood. He will give them to the fire.
chapters.16.lds: How does the comparison with Sodom challenge Jerusalem’s pride?
chapters.16.summary: God tells Ezekiel to show Jerusalem her history. She was an unwanted baby left in a field. God said, “Live,” and later married her and dressed her as a queen. She trusted her beauty and gave herself to other gods and nations. She even sacrificed her children. Her sisters Samaria and Sodom did less wrong than she did. Sodom was proud and well fed and did not help the poor. Yet God will remember his covenant and forgive her.
chapters.17.lds: Why does the vine’s search for another eagle become a broken obligation?
chapters.17.summary: God gives Ezekiel a riddle about two eagles and a vine. A great eagle takes the top of a cedar and plants a seed. The seed becomes a low vine that grows toward him. Then the vine stretches its roots toward a second eagle. God explains that Babylon’s king took Judah’s king away. He made a treaty with a new king, who swore an oath. That king rebelled and sent to Egypt for horses. God will plant a tender shoot himself, and it will become a great cedar.
chapters.18.lds: How do the three generations challenge the sour-grapes saying?
chapters.18.summary: The people quote a proverb: the fathers ate sour grapes, and the children’s teeth ache. God says they will not use it any more. Every life belongs to him, and the one who sins will die. A righteous man will live. His violent son will die for his own acts. That man’s son, if he does right, will live. A wicked person who turns will live, and his wrongs will not be remembered. God says he takes no pleasure in anyone’s death.
chapters.19.lds: Why does the song combine royal strength with capture and burning?
chapters.19.summary: Ezekiel sings a funeral song for the princes of Israel. Their mother was a lioness who raised her cubs. One cub became a young lion and was caught and taken to Egypt. Another prowled among the lions and was caged and taken to Babylon. Their mother was also like a vine with strong branches. It was pulled up in anger and planted in the desert. Fire came out from its own branch. No strong branch is left to be a ruler’s scepter.
chapters.20.lds: Why does this history repeat God’s concern for his name?
chapters.20.summary: Elders come to Ezekiel to ask something of the LORD. God refuses to be consulted by them. He tells Ezekiel to recount their fathers’ history. In Egypt, in the desert, and in the land, Israel rebelled. Each time God held back for the sake of his name. The people now think they will be like the nations and serve wood and stone. God says that will never happen. He will rule them, purge the rebels, and bring them to his holy mountain.
chapters.21.lds: Why does dismissing the foreign ruler’s choice fail to protect Jerusalem?
chapters.21.summary: God says his sword is drawn against Jerusalem, and Ezekiel must groan aloud. The sword is sharpened and polished. Ezekiel marks out two roads for the king of Babylon. One leads to the Ammonite capital and one to Jerusalem. The king stops at the fork and uses arrows, idols, and a liver to decide. The lot falls on Jerusalem. Judah’s prince must take off his crown. It will be given to the one who has the right to it.
chapters.22.lds: How do abuses against poor people connect with failures in worship?
chapters.22.summary: God calls Jerusalem a city of bloodshed. Its princes use their power to kill. People dishonor parents and wrong the foreigner, the orphan, and the widow. They take bribes and interest and have forgotten God. Israel has become like the waste left when metal is melted. Prophets, priests, and officials all devour the people. The common people also rob the poor and the foreigner. God looked for one person to stand in the gap and found none.
chapters.23.lds: What changes when the cities’ desired allies become their attackers?
chapters.23.summary: God tells a story of two sisters, Samaria and Jerusalem. Both were unfaithful from their youth in Egypt. Samaria desired the Assyrians and was handed over to them. Jerusalem saw this and did worse. She desired the Assyrians and then the Babylonians. God will bring those lovers against her as attackers. She must drink her sister’s cup of ruin. The sisters are charged with idolatry and with sacrificing their children.
chapters.24.lds: Why do the people ask about Ezekiel’s unusual response to loss?
chapters.24.summary: On the day Babylon’s siege begins, God tells Ezekiel to record the date. He gives a parable of a cooking pot that cannot be cleaned. Then God says he will take away the delight of Ezekiel’s eyes. Ezekiel must not mourn or weep. His wife dies that evening, and he does as he was told. The people ask what this means for them. God says he will take his sanctuary, the delight of their eyes. They will be too stunned to mourn, as Ezekiel was.
chapters.25.lds: Why does celebrating Judah’s loss become a charge against its neighbors?
chapters.25.summary: God speaks against four neighbors of Judah. Ammon gloated when the temple was profaned and Judah went into exile. Ammon clapped, stamped, and rejoiced with contempt. Moab said Judah was like every other nation. Edom took revenge on Judah. The Philistines acted with old hatred. God will hand Ammon and Moab to the peoples of the east. He will lay his hand on Edom and the Philistines.
chapters.26.lds: How does hoped-for profit from Jerusalem’s fall reverse in the warning?
chapters.26.summary: God speaks against the trading city of Tyre. Tyre gloated when Jerusalem fell. It expected to grow rich now that a rival gate was broken. God will bring many nations against it like waves. Nebuchadnezzar will come with horses, chariots, and siege works. Tyre’s wealth and goods will be plundered. Its stones and timber will be thrown into the sea. The rulers of the coast will tremble and sing a lament.
chapters.27.lds: How does the list of trading partners increase the scale of loss?
chapters.27.summary: God tells Ezekiel to sing a lament for Tyre. The city is pictured as a beautiful ship. Its planks, mast, oars, and sail come from many lands. Men of many nations row it and guard it. A long list names its trading partners and their goods. The cargo includes metals, horses, ivory, wheat, wine, and slaves. An east wind breaks the ship in the heart of the sea. Sailors and merchants weep at its fall.
chapters.28.lds: Why does the ruler’s wealth fail to support his claim to divinity?
chapters.28.summary: God speaks to the ruler of Tyre, who says he is a god. He is a man, though he is wise and has grown rich. Foreigners will kill him, and he will not claim to be a god then. A lament follows for the king of Tyre. He was in Eden, covered with precious stones. He was blameless until wrong was found in him. Trade filled him with violence, and beauty made him proud. A short message then promises Israel a safe home.
chapters.29.lds: How does the later speech distinguish effort against Tyre from expected payment?
chapters.29.summary: God speaks against Pharaoh, the great monster lying in the Nile. Pharaoh says the river is his and he made it. God will put hooks in his jaws and leave him in the desert. Egypt was a reed staff that broke when Israel leaned on it. The land will be desolate for forty years. Then Egypt will return as a lowly kingdom. A later message says Nebuchadnezzar got no wages from Tyre. God will give him Egypt as his pay.
chapters.30.lds: What does the broken-arm comparison say about expected military help?
chapters.30.summary: God says a day of clouds is near for Egypt. The sword will come, and Egypt’s allies will fall with it. Nebuchadnezzar will destroy the land. God will end the idols of Memphis and judge Egypt’s cities by name. At Tahpanhes the day will grow dark. A second message says God has broken Pharaoh’s arm. It has not been bound up to hold a sword. God will strengthen the arms of Babylon’s king.
chapters.31.lds: Why does Pharaoh hear a warning through another power’s tree?
chapters.31.summary: God asks Pharaoh whom he resembles in his greatness. Assyria was a cedar of Lebanon, taller than every tree. Deep waters fed it, and birds nested in its branches. All great nations lived in its shade. Because it grew proud of its height, God gave it to a ruthless nation. Foreigners cut it down, and its branches fell on the hills. It went down to the grave. Pharaoh and his many people will be brought down the same way.
chapters.32.lds: How does shared burial reverse the nations’ former terror?
chapters.32.summary: Ezekiel sings a lament for Pharaoh. He thought himself a lion, but he is a monster that muddies the rivers. God will catch him in a net and darken the sky over him. Then Ezekiel is told to wail for Egypt’s crowds. They go down to the pit with other fallen nations. Assyria is there, and Elam, Meshech, Tubal, Edom, and the Sidonians. Each once spread terror in the land of the living. Pharaoh will see them and be consoled over his own army.
chapters.33.lds: The lesson studies repentance as a change of conduct that can lead to life. Why does enjoying the prophet’s voice fail to answer his message?
chapters.33.summary: God again makes Ezekiel a watchman for Israel. The people say their sins weigh on them and they are wasting away. God says he takes no pleasure in the death of the wicked. A wicked person who turns and makes things right will live. A man escapes from Jerusalem and reports that the city has fallen. Those left in the ruins claim the land, and God rejects their claim. The exiles now come to hear Ezekiel. They listen as to a love song and do not act.
chapters.34.lds: The lesson connects the shepherd’s care with following the Savior. Why must care for wounded sheep include judgment against stronger sheep?
chapters.34.summary: God speaks against Israel’s shepherds, who feed themselves. They do not strengthen the weak, heal the sick, or search for the lost. The flock is scattered and has become food for wild animals. God says he himself will search for his sheep. He will bring them home and feed them on good pasture. He will also judge between one sheep and another. The strong have shoved the weak and fouled the water. He will set one shepherd over them, his servant David.
chapters.35.lds: How does God’s presence challenge Seir’s claim to empty land?
chapters.35.summary: God tells Ezekiel to speak against Mount Seir, the land of Edom. Edom kept an old hatred and gave Israelites to the sword in their disaster. So bloodshed will pursue Edom. Edom said the two nations and their lands would be its own. Yet the LORD was there. God heard every insult Edom spoke against Israel’s mountains. Edom rejoiced when Israel’s land lay empty. Its own land will be made empty.
chapters.36.lds: The lesson connects a new heart with repentance and obedience. Why does return require more than new homes and productive fields?
chapters.36.summary: God speaks to the mountains of Israel. Enemies have claimed them, and they will soon bear fruit for his people. Israel defiled the land and was scattered among the nations. There the people brought dishonor on God’s name. He will act for the sake of that name and bring them home. He will sprinkle clean water on them. He will give them a new heart and put his Spirit in them. The ruined land will become like the garden of Eden.
chapters.37.lds: The lesson also reads the sticks as the Bible and the Book of Mormon. This later Church interpretation differs from Ezekiel’s explanation of reunited peoples. Doctrine and Covenants 27:5 speaks of the record of the stick of Ephraim. How do the bones and sticks answer different forms of separation?
chapters.37.summary: The LORD sets Ezekiel in a valley full of dry bones. He asks whether the bones can live, and Ezekiel says only God knows. Ezekiel speaks, and the bones join and are covered with flesh. He speaks again, and breath enters them, and they stand. God says the bones are the whole house of Israel. He will bring them out of their graves to their land. Ezekiel joins two sticks marked for Judah and Joseph. God will make them one nation under one king.
chapters.38.lds: Why does the attacker treat peaceful villages as an opportunity?
chapters.38.summary: God speaks against Gog, a ruler from the far north. Gog leads a great army with many allies. In later years he will invade a land restored from war. Its people will be living safely in villages without walls. Gog plans to seize plunder from them. Merchants ask whether he has come for silver and gold. God says he will bring Gog there so that the nations may know him. Earthquake, sword, hail, and fire will meet the army.
chapters.39.lds: How do fuel and burial work reverse the invader’s display of strength?
chapters.39.summary: God says Gog will fall on the mountains of Israel. Birds and wild animals will feed on his army. Israel will burn the invaders’ weapons as fuel for seven years. They will bury the dead for seven months to cleanse the land. The nations will learn that Israel went into exile for its own sin. God hid his face from them then. Now he will restore Jacob and have mercy. He will pour out his Spirit and hide his face no more.
chapters.40.lds: Why does the guide require careful looking and listening before reporting?
chapters.40.summary: In the twenty-fifth year of exile, God brings Ezekiel in a vision to Israel. On a high mountain he sees buildings like a city. A man who shines like bronze holds a measuring rod. He tells Ezekiel to look, listen, and pay close attention. He measures the outer wall and the east gate with its guardrooms. He measures the outer court and its other gates. He measures the inner court and the tables for offerings. He names the rooms for the priests who serve.
chapters.41.lds: How do different entrances mark the movement toward the most holy place?
chapters.41.summary: The guide brings Ezekiel into the main hall of the temple and measures it. He goes alone into the inner room and measures it. He says, “This is the most holy place.” Side rooms stand in three stories around the house. A large building lies to the west. The walls are paneled with wood and carved with cherubim and palm trees. Each cherub has a human face and a lion’s face. A wooden altar stands before the inner room.
chapters.42.lds: Why must priests change garments before approaching the people’s area?
chapters.42.summary: The guide shows Ezekiel two blocks of rooms beside the temple. They stand three stories high with walkways in front. Priests who come near the LORD eat the most holy offerings there. They store the offerings in those rooms. They must leave their service clothes there before going to the outer court. They put on other clothes to go where the people are. The guide then measures the whole area. A wall around it separates the holy from the common.
chapters.43.lds: How does the return of glory answer its earlier departure?
chapters.43.summary: The guide brings Ezekiel to the east gate. The glory of Israel’s God comes from the east with a sound like rushing water. Ezekiel knows it as the glory he saw before, and he falls on his face. The glory enters the temple and fills it. A voice says this is the place of God’s throne. He will live there among Israel forever. The people must put away their old defilements. Ezekiel then receives the measurements and rites of the altar.
chapters.44.lds: How does the teaching duty answer the earlier charge against priests?
chapters.44.summary: The east gate stays shut, since the LORD has entered by it. Only the prince may sit there to eat. God rebukes Israel for letting unfaithful foreigners serve in his house. Levites who went after idols may serve only as gatekeepers and helpers. The sons of Zadok, who stayed faithful, will come near as priests. They wear linen, trim their hair, and drink no wine before serving. They must teach the people the difference between holy and common. They own no land, for God is their inheritance.
chapters.45.lds: Why do assigned royal land and honest measures belong together?
chapters.45.summary: The land is to be divided, with a holy district set apart for the LORD. It holds the sanctuary and land for priests and Levites. The city receives its own portion. The prince receives land on both sides of the holy district. God tells the princes to stop their violence and stop evicting his people. They must use honest scales and honest measures. The people bring set offerings to the prince. He provides the sacrifices at feasts and Sabbaths.
chapters.46.lds: How does the inheritance rule restrain the prince’s power?
chapters.46.summary: The inner east gate opens on Sabbaths and new moons. The prince worships at the threshold of the gate and does not go farther. The people worship at the entrance. At the feasts each person leaves by the gate opposite the one he entered. The prince goes in and out among them. A lamb is offered every morning. The prince may give land to his sons only from his own estate. The chapter ends with the kitchens where offerings are cooked.
chapters.47.lds: The lesson reads the healing river through blessings associated with temple worship. How does inheritance for resident foreigners extend the promise of restored life?
chapters.47.summary: Water flows from under the temple’s threshold toward the east. The guide measures it four times, and it deepens from ankle to a river. Trees grow thick on both banks. The water runs down to the Dead Sea and makes it fresh. Fish swarm there, and fishermen spread their nets. The trees bear fruit every month, and their leaves heal. God then gives the borders of the land. Foreigners who settle there receive an inheritance with the tribes.
chapters.48.lds: Why does the book end by naming the city’s relationship with God?
chapters.48.summary: The land is divided among the tribes in strips from north to south. Seven tribes lie north of the holy district. The district holds the sanctuary, the priests, and the Levites. The city lies beside it, and workers from every tribe farm its land. The prince’s land lies on either side. Five tribes lie to the south. The city has twelve gates, each named for a tribe. From that day the city’s name is “The LORD is there.”
